edges.effect_quant: Across cohort syntheses, longer lactation is associated with lower later maternal type 2 diabetes risk. A 2014 dose-response meta-analysis of six cohort studies involving 273,961 women found a pooled RR of 0.91 (95% CI 0.86 to 0.96) per additional year of total breastfeeding, and large US and Australian cohorts also found progressively lower diabetes risk with longer lactation.
edges.population: parous women followed for later type 2 diabetes after varying lifetime breastfeeding durations
edges.mechanism: Lactation increases energy expenditure and may improve postpartum glucose disposal, insulin sensitivity, beta-cell demand, and body-fat distribution. These physiologic changes offer a plausible pathway by which longer breastfeeding might reduce long-term diabetes risk, especially after pregnancies characterized by insulin resistance.
edges.summary: The observational evidence consistently leans protective. Longer breastfeeding duration is associated with lower maternal type 2 diabetes risk later in life, and the relationship appears graded across multiple cohort-based syntheses.
edges.caveats: Residual confounding remains possible because women who breastfeed longer may differ in metabolic health, adiposity, smoking, and social conditions. Some shorter-term studies in women with gestational diabetes have been mixed, but the longer follow-up literature is more consistently protective.

evidence.citation: Aune et al 2014 Nutr Metab Cardiovasc Dis
evidence.notes: Breastfeeding and the maternal risk of type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of cohort studies.
